original_value: The automatic detection of pulse during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is necessary for the early recognition of the arrest and the detection of return of spontaneous circulation (end of the arrest). The only signal available in every single defibrillator and valid for the detection of pulse is the electrocardiogram (ECG). In this study we propose two deep neural network (DNN) architectures to detect pulse using short ECG segments (5 s), i.e., to classify the rhythm into pulseless electrical activity (PEA) or pulse-generating rhythm (PR). A total of 3914 5-s ECG segments, 2372 PR and 1542 PEA, were extracted from 279 OHCA episodes. Data were partitioned patient-wise into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The first DNN architecture was a fully convolutional neural network, and the second architecture added a recurrent layer to learn temporal dependencies. Both DNN architectures were tuned using Bayesian optimization, and the results for the test set were compared to state-of-the art PR/PEA discrimination algorithms based on machine learning and hand crafted features. The PR/PEA classifiers were evaluated in terms of sensitivity (Se) for PR, specificity (Sp) for PEA, and the balanced accuracy (BAC), the average of Se and Sp. The Se/Sp/BAC of the DNN architectures were 94.1%/92.9%/93.5% for the first one, and 95.5%/91.6%/93.5% for the second one. Both architectures improved the performance of state of the art methods by more than 1.5 points in BAC.

result.paraphrase: Automatic pulse detection during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is essential for early identification of the arrest and for recognizing return of spontaneous circulation, which marks the end of the arrest. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is the only signal available on every defibrillator and the only one validated for pulse detection. Here, we present two deep neural network (DNN) architectures for pulse detection from short ECG segments (5 s), classifying rhythms as pulseless electrical activity (PEA) or pulse-generating rhythm (PR). In total, 3914 5-s ECG segments were extracted from 279 OHCA episodes, including 2372 PR and 1542 PEA segments. Data were split by patient into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The first DNN was a fully convolutional neural network, and the second incorporated a recurrent layer to capture temporal dependencies. Both models were tuned with Bayesian optimization, and test-set performance was compared with state-of-the-art PR/PEA discrimination methods based on machine learning and handcrafted features. Performance was assessed using sensitivity (Se) for PR, specificity (Sp) for PEA, and balanced accuracy (BAC), defined as the average of Se and Sp. The Se/Sp/BAC values were 94.1%/92.9%/93.5% for the first architecture and 95.5%/91.6%/93.5% for the second. Both architectures outperformed state-of-the-art methods by more than 1.5 BAC points.
